MAC-001.q: Match each cost type with an example at a manufacturer:
p: Electricity with a fixed charge plus usage-based part
Project survey costs already spent, not recoverable
MAC-001.e: Classification by cost behaviour and decision relevance.
MAC-001.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (Horngren – Cost Accounting; CIMA); Circular 53/2006/TT-BTC.
Analysis: Variable costs move in proportion to output (direct materials); fixed costs stay constant within the relevant range (factory depreciation, plant supervisors' pay); mixed costs have fixed and variable parts (electricity with a fixed charge plus usage); sunk costs are spent and unrecoverable, irrelevant to decisions (MAC-002).

MAC-002.q: A sunk cost has been incurred in the past and cannot be changed by any decision, so it is not relevant for decision-making.
MAC-002.e: True. E.g., the purchase price of an old machine does not affect the decision to replace it.
MAC-002.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (relevant costs).
Analysis: True. Sunk costs are already incurred and unaffected by any future choice → irrelevant to decisions. E.g., the old machine's purchase price doesn't affect replacing it; only its disposal value (future, differing between options) is relevant. 'We've invested too much to stop' is the sunk-cost fallacy.

MAC-003.q: Opportunity cost is the benefit forgone by choosing one option over the best alternative; it is not recorded in financial accounting but must be considered in decisions.
MAC-003.e: True. E.g., using premises as a warehouse rather than leasing them out – the forgone rent is the opportunity cost.
MAC-003.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Analysis: True. Opportunity cost is the benefit forgone from the best alternative. With no transaction it isn't recorded in financial accounts, but it's a relevant cost in decisions. E.g., using premises as a warehouse instead of renting them out → the forgone rent belongs in the warehouse option's cost.

MAC-004.q: When are product costs (direct materials, direct labour, production overhead) recognised in the income statement?
o: When the product is sold (via cost of goods sold); before that they sit in inventory
As soon as the costs are incurred
At year-end whether sold or not
MAC-004.e: Only period costs (selling, administrative) are fully expensed in the period incurred.
MAC-004.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice; VAS 02 (inventory cost).
Analysis: Product costs (direct materials, direct labour, overheads) attach to products: they sit in inventory (accounts 154, 155) until sale, then go to COGS (632) – the matching principle.
Distractors: B fits period costs (selling, admin – expensed immediately); C and D don't follow the principle.

MAC-005.q: Using the high–low method: the highest month has 10,000 machine hours and maintenance cost of VND 80 million; the lowest month has 6,000 hours and 60 million. What is the variable maintenance cost per machine hour (VND)?
MAC-005.e: (80 − 60) million / (10,000 − 6,000) = 5,000 VND/hour; fixed cost = 80 − 10,000 × 5,000 = 30 million VND/month.
MAC-005.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (high–low method).
Working: Variable cost = (80 − 60) million / (10,000 − 6,000) hours = 20,000,000 / 4,000 = 5,000 VND per hour. Fixed cost = 80 million − 10,000 × 5,000 = 30 million a month. Equation: Y = 30 million + 5,000X.
Note: Using only 2 points, it's skewed by outliers; regression is more reliable.

MAC-006.q: Fixed cost per unit falls as volume rises (within the relevant range), while variable cost per unit stays constant.
MAC-006.e: True. This underlies economies of scale.
MAC-006.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Analysis: True. Total fixed costs are constant within the relevant range, so fixed cost per unit = total / output falls as output rises; variable cost per unit is constant while the total rises proportionally. This underlies economies of scale; beyond the range (extra shifts, new machines) fixed costs step up.

MAC-007.q: Select ALL items that are production overhead at a food processing plant:
o: Electricity, water and steam used in production
MAC-007.e: Advertising is a selling expense; directors' salaries are administrative expenses.
MAC-007.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice; Circular 99/2025/TT-BTC (account 627 – production overheads).
Analysis: Production overheads: (A) packaging line depreciation; (B) plant supervisor pay; (C) power, water and steam for production – incurred in the factory but not traceable to individual units.
Distractors: (D) advertising – selling expense (641); (E) directors' pay – administrative expense (642).

MAC-008.q: Management accounting provides information for internal management, need not follow accounting standards, and can be prepared for any period or format that suits management needs.
MAC-008.e: True. Circular 53/2006/TT-BTC guides management accounting in enterprises.
MAC-008.x:
Basis: Circular 53/2006/TT-BTC on applying management accounting; 2015 Accounting Law.
Analysis: True. Management accounting serves internal decisions: it isn't bound by accounting standards, and periods and formats suit needs (daily, weekly, by product or customer), emphasising the future and timeliness. Circular 53/2006 is guidance; firms organise it as suits them.

MAC-009.q: A case of product sells for VND 30,000 with variable cost of 18,000 per case. What is the unit contribution margin (VND)?
MAC-009.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (CVP analysis).
Working: Unit contribution margin = price − variable cost = 30,000 − 18,000 = 12,000 VND per case – each case's contribution to fixed costs and profit.

MAC-010.q: A carton sells for VND 30,000 with variable cost of 18,000 per carton. What is the contribution margin ratio (%)?
MAC-010.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Working: Contribution margin ratio = 12,000 / 30,000 = 40% – each 100 VND of sales contributes 40 to fixed costs.

MAC-011.q: Fixed costs are VND 600 million; unit contribution margin 12,000. What is the break-even volume (cases)?
MAC-011.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (break-even point).
Working: Break-even units = fixed costs / unit contribution = 600,000,000 / 12,000 = 50,000 cases.
Check: 50,000 × 12,000 = 600 million = fixed costs → zero profit.

MAC-012.q: Fixed costs are VND 600 million; contribution margin ratio 40%. What is break-even revenue (VND million)?
MAC-012.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Working: Break-even revenue = fixed costs / CM ratio = 600 / 40% = 1,500 million VND.
Check: 50,000 cases (MAC-011) × 30,000 = 1,500 million.

MAC-013.q: Fixed costs VND 600 million, unit contribution margin 12,000, target profit 240 million. How many cases must be sold?
MAC-013.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (target-profit volume).
Working: Units = (fixed costs + target profit) / unit contribution = (600 + 240) million / 12,000 = 840,000,000 / 12,000 = 70,000 cases.
Note: An after-tax target must be grossed up: pre-tax = after-tax / (1 − t).

MAC-014.q: Actual revenue is VND 2,000 million; break-even revenue 1,500 million. What is the margin of safety ratio (%)?
MAC-014.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (margin of safety).
Working: Margin of safety ratio = (actual − break-even sales) / actual = (2,000 − 1,500) / 2,000 = 25% – sales can fall 25% before losses.
Note: Margin of safety ratio = 1 / DOL (MAC-015).

MAC-015.q: Total contribution margin is VND 800 million; operating profit 200 million. What is the degree of operating leverage?
MAC-015.e: 800 / 200 = 4: a 10% rise in revenue raises profit by 40%.
MAC-015.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (operating leverage).
Working: DOL = total contribution / operating profit = 800 / 200 = 4 → a 10% rise in sales lifts profit 40% (and vice versa).
Note: Same as FIN-023; DOL is high near break-even.

MAC-016.q: Select ALL assumptions of CVP analysis:
o: Unit selling price is constant within the relevant range
Total fixed cost is constant within the relevant range
Production volume always differs from sales volume
MAC-016.e: CVP assumes production equals sales (constant inventory).
MAC-016.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (CVP assumptions).
Analysis: Assumptions: (A) constant unit price; (B) constant unit variable cost; (C) constant total fixed costs within the relevant range; (D) constant sales mix with multiple products (MAC-017).
Distractors: (E) CVP assumes production equals sales (no inventory change) – otherwise absorption-costing profit is affected (MAC-020).

MAC-017.q: With multiple products, break-even depends on the sales mix; increasing the share of high contribution-margin-ratio products lowers break-even revenue.
MAC-017.e: True. The weighted average contribution margin ratio rises.
MAC-017.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (multi-product CVP).
Analysis: True. Break-even sales = fixed costs / weighted average CM ratio, weighted by sales mix (MAC-055). Shifting mix toward high-CM products → higher average ratio → lower break-even sales. Pushing high-margin products matters as much as growing sales.

MAC-018.q: A business with a high share of fixed costs (high operating leverage) sees profits rise quickly once revenue exceeds break-even but losses mount quickly when revenue falls.
MAC-018.e: True. This is typical of automated plants, hotels and airlines.
MAC-018.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (cost structure and operating leverage).
Analysis: True. High fixed, low variable costs → large contribution margins and high DOL: above break-even almost every extra sale becomes profit; below it losses mount since fixed costs still fall due. Typical of automated plants, hotels, airlines – very sensitive to utilisation (FIN-026).

MAC-019.q: The main difference between absorption costing and variable costing is the treatment of:
MAC-019.e: Absorption costing includes fixed production overhead in product cost; variable costing expenses it as a period cost.
MAC-019.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice; VAS 02.
Analysis: The difference is fixed production overhead: absorption costing includes it in product cost (held in inventory until sold); variable costing treats it as a period cost, expensed in full.
Distractors: B and D – direct materials and labour are product costs under both; C – variable selling costs are period costs under both.

MAC-020.q: 10,000 units are produced and 8,000 sold; fixed production overhead VND 200 million; no opening inventory. By how much does absorption-costing profit exceed variable-costing profit (VND)?
MAC-020.e: Fixed overhead per unit = 20,000 VND; closing inventory of 2,000 units carries 40 million of fixed overhead → absorption profit is higher by 40,000,000 VND.
MAC-020.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (reconciling absorption and variable profit).
Working: Fixed overhead per unit = 200,000,000 / 10,000 = 20,000 VND. Closing stock = 10,000 − 8,000 = 2,000 units carrying 2,000 × 20,000 = 40,000,000 VND of fixed overhead → absorption profit exceeds variable by 40,000,000 VND.
Note: When sales exceed production (stock falls), absorption profit is lower.

MAC-021.q: Variable costing is convenient for CVP analysis and short-term decisions but cannot be used for financial statements under the standards.
MAC-021.e: True. VAS 02 requires inventory cost to include allocated fixed production overhead.
MAC-021.x:
Basis: VAS 02; management accounting practice.
Analysis: True. Variable costing separates variable and fixed costs, ideal for CVP, short-term pricing and special orders. But VAS 02 (and IAS 2) require inventory cost to include fixed production overheads allocated on normal capacity → financial statements must use absorption costing.

MAC-022.q: Activity-based costing (ABC) allocates production overhead based on:
o: The cost drivers of each activity
A single base such as labour hours
MAC-022.e: ABC better reflects costs of diverse products made in small batches.
MAC-022.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (Kaplan & Cooper – Activity-Based Costing).
Analysis: ABC pools overheads by activity (set-ups, inspections, order handling) and assigns them to products by each activity's cost driver (number of set-ups, inspections, orders) – more accurate for diverse, small-batch products.
Distractors: B is traditional single-base allocation; C and D don't reflect what causes the costs.

MAC-023.q: The 'machine setup' activity costs VND 120 million per year with 400 setups. What is the cost rate per setup (VND)?
MAC-023.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (ABC).
Working: Activity rate = 120,000,000 / 400 set-ups = 300,000 VND per set-up. A product needing 50 set-ups is charged 50 × 300,000 = 15 million VND.

MAC-024.q: A plant's total bottled-water production cost for the month is VND 3,000 million; output 500,000 litres. What is the cost per litre (VND)?
MAC-024.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (process costing – simple method).
Working: Unit cost = 3,000,000,000 / 500,000 = 6,000 VND per litre.
Note: It applies to homogeneous output with no (or stable) work in progress; otherwise convert WIP into equivalent units (MAC-028).

MAC-025.q: Joint costs of VND 600 million produce two joint products at the split-off point: X 30,000 litres and Y 10,000 litres. Using physical units, how much joint cost is allocated to X (VND million)?
MAC-025.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (joint cost allocation).
Working: X's share = 600 × 30,000 / (30,000 + 10,000) = 600 × 75% = 450 million VND; Y = 150 million.
Note: The physical-units method is simple but may overload low-value products; the sales-value-at-split-off method is often fairer.

MAC-026.q: Scrap and by-products sold by a factory (sawdust, fabric offcuts) are usually deducted from the main product's production cost or recognised as income.
MAC-026.e: True. The chosen method must be applied consistently.
MAC-026.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice; Circular 99/2025/TT-BTC.
Analysis: True. Low-value scrap and by-products (sawdust, fabric offcuts) sold are usually credited against main-product production cost or recorded as other income. The choice must be consistent; significant by-products should be treated as joint products.

MAC-027.q: Match each costing system with the suitable production type:
p: Continuous production of homogeneous products such as cement or beverages
Allocating overhead by each activity's cost driver
MAC-027.e: Mass producers of homogeneous goods mainly use process costing, possibly combined with ABC for overhead.
MAC-027.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Analysis: Job costing – custom orders, distinct batches (printing, shipbuilding, bespoke furniture); process costing – continuous, homogeneous output (cement, soft drinks); ABC – overheads by each activity's driver, combinable with either.

MAC-028.q: Under process costing, closing work-in-progress is converted into equivalent finished units to allocate costs.
MAC-028.e: True. Weighted average or FIFO can be used.
MAC-028.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (process costing).
Analysis: True. Closing work in progress is converted into equivalent finished units by its completion percentage for each cost element (e.g., 1,000 units 40% complete for conversion = 400 equivalent units). The weighted average (pooling opening WIP) or FIFO (separating work on opening WIP) method may be used.

MAC-029.q: Arrange the sequence for preparing a manufacturer's master budget:
o: Cost of sales, selling and administrative budgets
MAC-029.e: The sales budget comes first because it determines the scale of the other budgets.
MAC-029.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (master budget).
Analysis: Order: sales (the starting point that sets scale) → production (sales + closing − opening stock – MAC-061) → materials, labour, overheads → COGS, selling and admin → cash budget (CSH-027) → budgeted financial statements. Each step uses the previous outputs.

MAC-030.q: Match each budget type with its feature:
p: Prepared for a single expected activity level
Adjusted to the actual activity level
Every expenditure must be justified from scratch
Continuously adds a new period as one ends
MAC-030.e: The flexible budget is the basis for evaluating cost performance.
MAC-030.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Analysis: Static budget – one activity level; flexible budget – adjusted to actual activity, the fair yardstick for costs (MAC-031); zero-based budgeting (ZBB) – every spend justified from scratch, countering 'last year plus x%'; rolling budget – a new period added as each one ends.

MAC-031.q: Budgeted unit variable cost VND 10,000; fixed costs 100 million per month. Actual output 12,000 units. What is total cost under the flexible budget (VND million)?
MAC-031.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (flexible budget).
Working: Flexible budget cost = 12,000 × 10,000 + 100,000,000 = 120 + 100 = 220 million VND.
Note: Compare actual costs with 220 million (not the static budget at planned volume) to judge cost performance fairly.

MAC-032.q: 10,000 kg of material is bought at an actual price of VND 21,000/kg versus a standard of 20,000/kg. What is the material price variance (VND, adverse)?
MAC-032.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (standard cost variances).
Working: Price variance = actual quantity purchased × (actual − standard price) = 10,000 × (21,000 − 20,000) = 10,000,000 VND, adverse (above standard).
Note: Usually purchasing's responsibility; causes may be the market, rush orders or supplier changes.

MAC-033.q: Actual material used is 10,000 kg; standard quantity for actual output 9,500 kg; standard price VND 20,000/kg. What is the material usage variance (VND, adverse)?
MAC-033.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Working: Usage variance = standard price × (actual quantity − standard quantity for actual output) = 20,000 × (10,000 − 9,500) = 10,000,000 VND, adverse (more used than standard).
Note: Usually production's responsibility; the standard price isolates the price effect.

MAC-034.q: Actual labour hours 2,000 at an actual rate of VND 52,000/hour versus a standard 50,000/hour. What is the labour rate variance (VND, adverse)?
MAC-034.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Working: Labour rate variance = actual hours × (actual − standard rate) = 2,000 × (52,000 − 50,000) = 4,000,000 VND, adverse.
Note: Possible causes: regional minimum wage rises, overtime at 150–300%, higher-grade workers than standard.

MAC-035.q: Actual hours 2,000; standard hours for actual output 2,100; standard rate VND 50,000/hour. What is the labour efficiency variance (VND, favourable)?
MAC-035.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Working: Efficiency variance = standard rate × (standard − actual hours) = 50,000 × (2,100 − 2,000) = 5,000,000 VND, favourable (fewer hours than standard).
Check total labour variance: 4 million adverse + 5 million favourable = 1 million favourable (actual 104 million versus standard 105 million).

MAC-036.q: A favourable material price variance from buying poor-quality material may cause an adverse usage variance in production; variances should be analysed together.
MAC-036.e: True. Purchasing should not be judged on price variances alone.
MAC-036.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Analysis: True. Buying cheap, poor-quality material gives purchasing a favourable price variance but causes waste, scrap and downtime → adverse usage and efficiency variances in production, possibly exceeding the savings. Analyse variances together and avoid perverse incentives (don't judge purchasing on price alone).

MAC-037.q: Management by exception focuses investigation on significant variances above a threshold rather than every small variance.
MAC-037.e: True. Thresholds may be in % or absolute amounts.
MAC-037.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Analysis: True. Management by exception focuses attention on material variances above thresholds (a % like ±5% or an absolute amount), recurring trends, or unusual favourable variances (possibly wrong standards or recording errors) – rather than every small difference.

MAC-038.q: Select ALL possible causes of labour productivity (units per labour hour) below standard:
o: More idle time from material shortages
MAC-038.e: Selling price does not affect physical productivity.
MAC-038.x:
Basis: Management accounting and operations practice.
Analysis: Causes of low productivity: (A) poor materials causing stoppages; (B) breakdowns, missed maintenance; (C) untrained new workers; (E) idle time from material shortages.
Distractors: (D) Higher selling prices don't affect physical productivity (units per labour hour).

MAC-039.q: Making 10,000 packaging boxes in-house: variable cost VND 15,000 per box and avoidable fixed cost 50 million. Buying outside costs 18,000 per box. How much does buying save (VND)?
MAC-039.e: Make: 150 + 50 = 200 million; buy: 180 million; saving 20,000,000 VND (before qualitative factors).
MAC-039.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (make or buy).
Working: Make: variable 10,000 × 15,000 = 150 million + avoidable fixed 50 million = 200 million. Buy: 10,000 × 18,000 = 180 million. Buying saves 20,000,000 VND.
Note: Count only avoidable fixed costs; also weigh qualitative factors: quality, supply security, use of freed capacity.

MAC-040.q: With spare capacity, a customer offers to buy 5,000 extra cases at VND 25,000 per case; variable cost 18,000 per case, no extra fixed cost. What is the incremental profit from accepting (VND)?
MAC-040.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (special orders).
Working: With idle capacity and no added fixed costs → extra profit = (25,000 − 18,000) × 5,000 = 7,000 × 5,000 = 35,000,000 VND → accept.
Note: 25,000 is below the normal 30,000; consider effects on existing customers (price pressure) and competition rules.

MAC-041.q: When machine capacity is the limiting factor, the business should prioritise products with the:
o: Highest contribution margin per machine hour
MAC-041.e: E.g., A (12,000 VND/2 hours = 6,000 VND/hour) ranks above B (15,000 VND/3 hours = 5,000 VND/hour).
MAC-041.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (limiting factors).
Analysis: With machine hours as the constraint, prioritise the highest contribution per machine hour – maximising total contribution from limited capacity. E.g., A: 12,000/2 hours = 6,000 per hour > B: 15,000/3 hours = 5,000 per hour → prefer A despite its lower unit contribution.
Distractors: B, C and D ignore use of the scarce resource.

MAC-042.q: A decision to drop a loss-making segment should consider the segment's contribution margin and avoidable fixed costs; unavoidable allocated common costs should not be the basis.
MAC-042.e: True. Dropping a segment with positive segment margin can reduce company profit.
MAC-042.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (dropping a segment).
Analysis: True. A segment 'losing' after allocated common costs may still have a positive segment margin (contribution − avoidable traceable fixed costs). Dropping it removes only its contribution and avoidable fixed costs; unavoidable common costs remain, shifting to other segments → company profit may fall. Also consider effects on other products' sales (complements).

MAC-043.q: Match each responsibility centre with its main performance measure:
MAC-043.e: Responsibility accounting links measures to the manager's span of control.
MAC-043.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (responsibility accounting).
Analysis: Cost centre – actual versus flexible budget costs; revenue centre – actual versus budget revenue; profit centre – segment profit; investment centre – ROI, RI, EVA (MAC-044, MAC-045). Measures match the manager's span of control (MAC-074).

MAC-044.q: A division's operating profit is VND 30 billion; average invested capital 200 billion. What is the division's ROI (%)?
MAC-044.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (investment centres).
Working: ROI = operating profit / average invested capital = 30 / 200 = 15%.
Note: ROI = margin × capital turnover (DuPont for divisions).

MAC-045.q: A division earns operating profit of VND 30 billion on average invested capital of 200 billion; required minimum return 12%. What is residual income (RI) (VND billion)?
MAC-045.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Working: RI = operating profit − minimum rate × invested capital = 30 − 12% × 200 = 30 − 24 = 6 billion VND.
Note: RI is absolute and encourages any project returning > 12% (MAC-046); EVA is RI with accounting adjustments and WACC (FIN-030).

MAC-046.q: Evaluating performance by ROI may lead managers to reject projects returning more than the cost of capital but less than the division's current ROI; RI overcomes this.
MAC-046.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (goal incongruence).
Analysis: True. A division earning 15% ROI with a new project returning 13% (> 12% cost of capital) adds value for the company but lowers the division's average ROI → an ROI-judged manager may reject it. The project's RI = (13% − 12%) × capital > 0 → divisional RI rises → it's accepted, aligning with company interests.

MAC-047.q: The minimum transfer price the selling division should accept for internal sales is:
o: Unit variable cost plus unit opportunity cost (contribution lost on external sales)
Unit variable cost minus a discount
MAC-047.e: With spare capacity, opportunity cost is zero and the minimum is variable cost.
MAC-047.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (transfer pricing).
Analysis: Minimum transfer price = unit variable cost + unit opportunity cost (contribution lost on forgone external sales). With idle capacity → opportunity cost = 0 → minimum = variable cost. At full capacity → minimum ≈ market price (less selling costs saved internally).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't based on opportunity cost.

MAC-048.q: Match each Balanced Scorecard perspective with a sample measure at a retail chain:
p: Sales per m² of store space, stock-out rate
Training hours per employee, staff turnover
MAC-048.e: The BSC links strategy with balanced measures.
MAC-048.x:
Basis: Balanced Scorecard (Kaplan & Norton, 1992).
Analysis: Financial – gross margin, ROIC; customer – repeat rate, NPS; internal process – sales per m², stock-out rate; learning and growth – training hours per employee, staff turnover. The BSC links strategy through cause and effect: people → processes → customers → financials.

MAC-049.q: Match each quality cost category with an example:
p: Training workers on standard operating procedures
Scrapping a non-compliant batch at the plant
Recalling defective products from the market
MAC-049.e: Investing in prevention usually sharply reduces failure costs.
MAC-049.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (cost of quality – PAF model).
Analysis: Prevention – standard-procedure training, quality design; appraisal – material sampling, testing; internal failure – scrapping rejected batches, rework; external failure – market recalls, warranty, lost reputation. Prevention spending usually cuts failure costs sharply – especially external failures, the costliest.

MAC-050.q: Target cost equals the target selling price minus desired profit; the product is designed to achieve this cost.
MAC-050.e: True. Suitable for new products in price-competitive markets.
MAC-050.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (target costing).
Analysis: True. Target cost = market-set target price − desired profit; the product is designed backwards to meet it (value engineering, material choices, simpler processes). Unlike cost-plus (MAC-071), which starts from cost and adds margin. It suits new products in price-competitive markets (MAC-070).

MAC-051.q: Throughput accounting treats material cost as the only truly variable cost and maximises throughput per unit of time at the bottleneck.
MAC-051.e: True. It is based on the Theory of Constraints (TOC).
MAC-051.x:
Basis: Throughput accounting; Theory of Constraints (Goldratt – The Goal).
Analysis: True. Throughput accounting treats materials as the only truly variable cost in the short term; labour and overheads are fixed operating expenses. Throughput = sales − materials; prioritise products with the highest throughput per bottleneck hour, since bottleneck capacity sets the whole system's output (MAC-073).

MAC-052.q: Useful management reports should be timely, tailored to users, focused on key measures and explain causes of variances – not merely present numbers.
MAC-052.e: True. Management reports serve decisions, so timeliness takes priority over absolute precision.
MAC-052.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (CIMA – Global Management Accounting Principles).
Analysis: True. Useful management reports are timely (data by the 5th of next month beats perfect data on the 25th), user-specific (plant manager versus board), focused on key metrics, and explain variances with recommended actions – not just tables of numbers.

MAC-053.q: Select ALL key operating KPIs commonly tracked in a transport–logistics company's management reports:
o: Rate of damaged or lost goods
MAC-053.e: Number of shareholders is not an operating KPI.
MAC-053.x:
Basis: Management accounting and logistics practice.
Analysis: Logistics operating KPIs: (A) on-time delivery (OTD); (B) fuel cost per km; (C) fleet utilisation, empty-running rate; (D) damage and loss rate.
Distractors: (E) Shareholder count says nothing about operations.

MAC-054.q: Revenue is VND 1,000 million; total variable costs 650 million. What is the contribution margin ratio (%)?
MAC-054.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (CVP – BAN-051, BAN-052).
Working: Contribution = 1,000 − 650 = 350 million; CM ratio = 350 / 1,000 = 35%.
Analysis: Each 100 of revenue contributes 35 toward fixed costs and profit. Break-even revenue = fixed costs / 35% (e.g., fixed costs 280 → break-even 800). A high ratio → profit is revenue-sensitive (operating leverage – BAN-055).
Check: 1,000 × 35% = 350 ✓.

MAC-055.q: A garment company sells two product groups: shirts (CM ratio 40%, 60% of revenue) and trousers (25%, 40% of revenue). What is the weighted average CM ratio (%)?
MAC-055.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (multi-product CVP).
Working: Weighted CM ratio = 40% × 60% + 25% × 40% = 24% + 10% = 34%.
Note: With fixed costs of 340 million, break-even sales = 340 / 34% = 1,000 million; more shirts in the mix lowers break-even (MAC-017).

MAC-056.q: Unit contribution margin VND 12,000, fixed costs 600 million, sales 80,000 cases. What is operating profit (VND million)?
MAC-056.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Working: Profit = 80,000 × 12,000 − 600,000,000 = 960 − 600 = 360 million VND.
Check: 30,000 cases above break-even (MAC-011) × 12,000 = 360 million.

MAC-057.q: Relevant costs for decisions are future costs that differ between alternatives.
MAC-057.e: True. Sunk costs and costs identical across alternatives are irrelevant.
MAC-057.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (relevant costs).
Analysis: True. Relevant costs meet two tests: future and differing between options. Irrelevant: sunk costs (past – MAC-002) and future costs identical across options (e.g., factory rent that's the same whichever option is chosen).

MAC-058.q: Fruit juice concentrate at split-off sells for VND 10,000/litre; further processed into bottled juice it sells for 16,000/litre (equivalent), with further processing cost of 4,000/litre. For 50,000 litres, what is the incremental profit from processing further (VND)?
MAC-058.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (sell or process further).
Working: Incremental profit per litre = extra revenue (16,000 − 10,000) − extra processing 4,000 = 2,000 VND. For 50,000 litres: 2,000 × 50,000 = 100,000,000 VND → process further.
Note: Joint costs before split-off are irrelevant (MAC-059).

MAC-059.q: Joint costs incurred before the split-off point are irrelevant to the sell-or-process-further decision.
MAC-059.e: True. Compare only incremental revenue with further processing cost.
MAC-059.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Analysis: True. Joint costs before split-off are incurred whether products are sold or processed further → they don't differ between options → irrelevant. Compare only incremental revenue with further processing costs (MAC-058). Allocating joint costs serves inventory valuation, not decisions.

MAC-060.q: Planned production 10,000 units at 2 kg of material per unit; desired closing material inventory 3,000 kg, opening 2,000 kg. How much material must be purchased (kg)?
MAC-060.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (materials purchase budget).
Working: Purchases = production needs + desired closing − opening stock = 10,000 × 2 + 3,000 − 2,000 = 20,000 + 1,000 = 21,000 kg.

MAC-061.q: Expected sales 50,000 cases; desired closing finished goods 5,000 cases; opening 4,000. How many cases must be produced?
MAC-061.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (production budget).
Working: Production = budgeted sales + desired closing − opening stock = 50,000 + 5,000 − 4,000 = 51,000 cases.

MAC-062.q: Actual sales 12,000 cases versus budget 10,000; budgeted unit contribution margin VND 12,000. What is the sales volume variance (VND, favourable)?
MAC-062.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (sales volume variance).
Working: Volume variance = (actual − budget units) × budgeted unit contribution = (12,000 − 10,000) × 12,000 = 24,000,000 VND, favourable.
Note: Budgeted contribution isolates the volume effect from price (MAC-063).

MAC-063.q: 12,000 cases are sold at an actual price of VND 29,000 versus a budget of 30,000. What is the sales price variance (VND, adverse)?
MAC-063.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (sales price variance).
Working: Price variance = actual units × (budget − actual price) = 12,000 × (30,000 − 29,000) = 12,000,000 VND, adverse.
Note: With MAC-062: the 1,000 price cut may have driven the extra 2,000 cases – a net 24 − 12 = 12 million favourable.

MAC-064.q: Budgeted production overhead is VND 400 million; budgeted machine hours 20,000. What is the overhead absorption rate (VND per machine hour)?
MAC-064.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (predetermined overhead rate).
Working: Rate = 400,000,000 / 20,000 machine hours = 20,000 VND per machine hour.
Note: A predetermined rate gives timely costing during the period; over- or under-absorption is cleared at period end (MAC-065).

MAC-065.q: Absorption rate VND 20,000 per machine hour; actual machine hours 22,000; actual overhead 420 million. What is over-absorbed overhead (VND)?
MAC-065.e: Absorbed 22,000 × 20,000 = 440 million; actual 420 million → over-absorbed 20,000,000 VND.
MAC-065.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Working: Absorbed = 22,000 × 20,000 = 440 million; actual 420 million → over-absorbed 440 − 420 = 20,000,000 VND; at period end, reduce COGS (or prorate to stock and COGS if material).

MAC-066.q: Under variable costing, profit moves with sales volume; under absorption costing, profit is also affected by production volume because fixed costs sit in inventory.
MAC-066.e: True. Overproducing to 'push' fixed costs into inventory can flatter short-term profit.
MAC-066.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Analysis: True. Variable costing expenses fixed production overheads in the period → profit depends only on sales volume. Absorption costing holds them in stock → producing more than is sold 'parks' fixed costs in inventory, boosting current profit (MAC-020). It's a short-term profit-dressing risk – analysts should watch for unusual stock build-ups.

MAC-067.q: Kaizen costing focuses on continuous small cost reductions during production; target costing focuses on the product design stage.
MAC-067.e: True. The two tools complement each other in strategic cost management.
MAC-067.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (Japanese cost management).
Analysis: True. Target costing operates at design – where most (about 70–80%) of life-cycle cost is locked in (MAC-050). Kaizen costing operates during production – continuous small reductions via process improvement and worker suggestions. The two complement each other.

MAC-068.q: Life-cycle costing tracks all costs from research, design and production to after-sales service and disposal.
MAC-068.e: True. It helps assess profitability over the product's entire life.
MAC-068.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (life-cycle costing).
Analysis: True. Life-cycle costing tracks all costs from research, design, production and marketing to after-sales service, take-back and disposal – not just annual production cost. It shows whole-life profitability and avoids underpricing products with big R&D or warranty costs.

MAC-069.q: Select ALL characteristics of a good KPI (SMART):
MAC-069.e: Too many KPIs dilute management focus.
MAC-069.x:
Basis: Management practice (SMART criteria – Doran, 1981).
Analysis: Good KPIs are: (A) specific; (B) measurable; (C) achievable; (D) relevant to strategic goals; (E) time-bound.
Distractors: (F) Too many KPIs dilute focus; pick a few key, strategy-linked metrics (BSC – MAC-048).

MAC-070.q: The target selling price of a new beverage product is VND 50,000; desired profit 20% of price. What is the target cost (VND)?
MAC-070.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (target costing).
Working: Target cost = 50,000 × (1 − 20%) = 40,000 VND. If the initial estimate is 45,000 → a 5,000 gap must be closed through design.

MAC-071.q: Unit cost VND 40,000; cost-plus pricing with a 25% markup on cost. What is the selling price (VND)?
MAC-071.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (cost-plus pricing).
Working: Price = 40,000 × (1 + 25%) = 50,000 VND.
Note: A 25% markup on cost equals a 20% margin on price (10,000/50,000) – markup and margin are easily confused.

MAC-072.q: When a competitive market exists for the intermediate product, market price is usually an appropriate basis for internal transfer pricing.
MAC-072.e: True. It enables fair evaluation of divisional performance.
MAC-072.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (transfer pricing); Decree 132/2020/ND-CP (arm's length principle for related parties).
Analysis: True. With a competitive market for the intermediate product, market price reflects opportunity cost (MAC-047), lets buying and selling divisions be judged fairly, and fits the tax arm's-length principle when divisions are related legal entities.

MAC-073.q: Throughput (revenue − materials) per bottleneck hour is VND 300,000; factory operating cost per hour is 200,000. What is the throughput accounting (TA) ratio?
MAC-073.x:
Basis: Throughput accounting (MAC-051).
Working: TA ratio = throughput per bottleneck hour / operating expense per hour = 300,000 / 200,000 = 1.5 > 1 → the product is profitable.
Note: TA < 1 means each bottleneck hour spent on the product doesn't cover the plant's operating expense.

MAC-074.q: Under responsibility accounting, cost centre managers should mainly be evaluated on:
o: All costs allocated from the company
MAC-074.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (controllability principle).
Analysis: Cost-centre managers should be judged mainly on costs they control (decide or significantly influence). Judging them on uncontrollable allocated company costs is unfair and demotivating.
Distractors: B, C and D are outside a cost centre's control.

MAC-075.q: A plant has 550 direct workers; in September (30 working days) it produced 495,000 units. What is average productivity (units per worker per day)?
MAC-075.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (labour productivity).
Working: Productivity = 495,000 / (550 × 30) = 495,000 / 16,500 = 30 units per worker per day.
Note: Compare with standard and prior periods; read with scrap rates so productivity isn't bought at the cost of quality.

MAC-076.q: Which is an example of a step cost?
MAC-076.e: A step cost is fixed within a range of activity, then jumps to a new level when a threshold is crossed.
o: Shift supervisor pay: each extra production shift needs another supervisor
MAC-076.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (cost behaviour).
Analysis: Step costs stay fixed over a range then jump when a threshold is crossed – shift supervisors' pay: each extra shift needs another supervisor.
Distractors: B is variable; C is fixed within the relevant range; D varies with sales.
Note: When planning higher output, identify step thresholds (extra shifts, trucks, warehouses).

MAC-077.q: Maintenance cost function: y = VND 30 million + 5,000 × machine hours. At 8,000 machine hours, what is the expected maintenance cost (VND million)?
MAC-077.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (mixed cost function).
Working: y = 30 million + 5,000 × 8,000 = 30 + 40 = 70 million VND.
Note: The function is reliable only within the data range used to estimate it (e.g., 6,000–10,000 hours – MAC-005).

MAC-078.q: Discretionary fixed costs (advertising, training) can be adjusted by management in the short term, while committed fixed costs (depreciation, long-term rent) stem from past investment decisions and are hard to change short term.
MAC-078.e: True. Cutting discretionary costs helps short-term profit but may harm long-term capability.
MAC-078.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (discretionary versus committed fixed costs).
Analysis: True. Discretionary fixed costs (advertising, training, R&D) are set periodically and adjustable short term; committed fixed costs (depreciation, long leases, key management pay) stem from past investment decisions and are hard to change quickly. Cutting discretionary costs flatters short-term profit but may damage long-term competitiveness.

MAC-079.q: Which cost is controllable by a workshop supervisor?
MAC-079.e: Controllable costs are those the manager can influence during the period.
o: Quantity of materials consumed in the workshop
MAC-079.x:
Basis: Responsibility accounting (controllability principle – MAC-074).
Analysis: Material usage in the plant is directly affected by the supervisor's decisions and oversight (standards, waste, scrap) → controllable.
Distractors: B, C and D are decided at company level; the supervisor can't influence them in the period.

MAC-080.e: Direct materials and production machine depreciation are product costs held in inventory until sale.
MAC-080.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (product versus period costs).
Analysis: Period costs are expensed when incurred: (A) sales commissions; (B) administrative pay; (C) advertising – selling and admin costs.
Distractors: (D) direct materials and (E) production machine depreciation are product costs, held in stock until sold (MAC-004).

MAC-081.q: Total cost is VND 260 million at 4,000 units and 340 million at 6,000 units. What is total fixed cost (VND million)?
MAC-081.e: Unit variable cost = (340 − 260) / 2,000 = 0.04 million = 40,000 VND; fixed = 260 − 4,000 × 0.04 = 100 million VND.
MAC-081.x:
Basis: High–low method.
Working: Unit variable cost = (340 − 260) / (6,000 − 4,000) = 80 / 2,000 = 0.04 million = 40,000 VND. Fixed cost = 260 − 4,000 × 0.04 = 260 − 160 = 100 million VND.
Check: 100 + 6,000 × 0.04 = 340.

MAC-082.q: Avoidable costs are relevant; unavoidable costs (incurred whichever option is chosen) are irrelevant to the decision.
MAC-082.e: True. This is a core principle in drop/keep and make/buy decisions.
MAC-082.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (relevant costs).
Analysis: True. Avoidable costs (eliminated by choosing an option or dropping a segment) differ between options → relevant. Unavoidable costs occur whatever is chosen → irrelevant. Core to drop/keep (MAC-042, MAC-126) and make/buy (MAC-039) decisions.

MAC-083.q: Match each cost term with its definition:
MAC-083.e: Understanding these terms helps identify relevant costs.
p: Difference in total cost between two options
Eliminated if an option/segment is dropped
Arises from past decisions, hard to change short term
Set periodically by management, e.g., advertising, R&D
MAC-083.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice.
Analysis: Incremental cost – the difference in total cost between two options; avoidable cost – eliminated if an option or segment is dropped; committed cost – arising from past decisions, hard to change short term; discretionary cost – set periodically by managers, like advertising and R&D (MAC-078).

MAC-084.q: Prime cost comprises direct materials and direct labour; conversion cost comprises direct labour and production overhead.
MAC-084.e: True. Direct labour appears in both.
MAC-084.x:
Basis: Cost accounting practice.
Analysis: True. Prime cost = direct materials + direct labour (direct costs); conversion cost = direct labour + overheads (cost of turning materials into product). Direct labour appears in both – don't add the two to get total production cost.

MAC-085.q: Direct materials 300 million, direct labour 200 million, production overhead 150 million VND. What is conversion cost (VND million)?
MAC-085.x:
Basis: Cost accounting practice.
Working: Conversion cost = direct labour 200 + overheads 150 = 350 million VND. Prime cost = 300 + 200 = 500; total production cost = 300 + 200 + 150 = 650.

MAC-086.q: Price VND 50,000 per unit, variable cost 30,000, fixed costs 400 million. What is break-even volume (units)?
MAC-086.x:
Basis: CVP analysis.
Working: Unit contribution = 50,000 − 30,000 = 20,000. Break-even units = 400,000,000 / 20,000 = 20,000 units.

MAC-087.q: Price VND 50,000/unit, variable cost 30,000 (contribution 20,000), fixed costs 400 million. Target AFTER-tax profit 160 million, tax 20%. How many units must be sold?
MAC-087.e: Required pre-tax profit = 160 / 0.8 = 200 million; volume = (400 + 200) million / 20,000 = 30,000 units.
MAC-087.x:
Basis: CVP analysis (after-tax target profit).
Working: Required pre-tax profit = 160 / (1 − 20%) = 200 million. Units = (400 + 200) million / 20,000 = 600,000,000 / 20,000 = 30,000 units.
Note: A common error is adding 160 million directly to fixed costs → 28,000 units, 2,000 short.

MAC-088.q: CM ratio 40%. Fixed costs rise from 600 to 720 million VND. What is the new break-even revenue (VND million)?
MAC-088.x:
Basis: CVP analysis.
Working: New break-even sales = 720 / 40% = 1,800 million VND (300 million above 1,500 – MAC-012); each extra unit of fixed cost needs 2.5 units of sales to break even.

MAC-089.q: Two products sold in a unit mix A:B = 3:1. Unit contribution A VND 10,000, B 30,000; fixed costs 300 million. What is the break-even volume of A (units)?
MAC-089.e: Contribution per 'bundle' (3A + 1B) = 30,000 + 30,000 = 60,000; break-even bundles = 300 million / 60,000 = 5,000; A = 15,000, B = 5,000.
MAC-089.x:
Basis: Multi-product CVP (sales-mix 'basket' method).
Working: Contribution per basket (3A + 1B) = 3 × 10,000 + 1 × 30,000 = 60,000. Break-even baskets = 300,000,000 / 60,000 = 5,000. A = 3 × 5,000 = 15,000 units; B = 5,000.
Check: 15,000 × 10,000 + 5,000 × 30,000 = 150 + 150 = 300 million = fixed costs.

MAC-090.q: Reducing unit variable cost (price and fixed costs unchanged) lowers break-even volume.
MAC-090.e: True. Unit contribution rises, so fewer units are needed to cover fixed costs.
MAC-090.x:
Basis: CVP analysis.
Analysis: True. Break-even units = fixed costs / (price − unit variable cost); lower variable cost → higher unit contribution → fewer units needed. E.g., MAC-086: variable cost down from 30,000 to 25,000 → break-even = 400 million / 25,000 = 16,000 units.

MAC-091.q: Raising the selling price while costs are unchanged makes break-even volume:
MAC-091.e: Unit contribution rises; but the effect of price on demand must be considered.
MAC-091.x:
Basis: CVP analysis.
Analysis: A higher price with unchanged costs → higher unit contribution → lower break-even volume.
Distractors: B, C and D go the wrong way.
Note: CVP assumes demand doesn't respond to price; in reality a price rise may cut demand (elasticity – MAC-138), so judge total profit, not just break-even.

MAC-092.q: Degree of operating leverage is 4. If revenue rises 5%, by how much (%) does operating profit rise?
MAC-092.x:
Basis: CVP analysis (operating leverage).
Working: % change in profit = DOL × % change in sales = 4 × 5% = 20%.
Note: Conversely, a 5% sales fall cuts profit 20%; DOL itself changes with the sales level.

MAC-093.q: Sales 70,000 cases, break-even 50,000 cases, unit contribution VND 12,000. What is operating profit (VND million)?
MAC-093.e: Profit = margin-of-safety units × unit contribution = 20,000 × 12,000 = 240 million VND.
MAC-093.x:
Basis: CVP analysis.
Working: Safety volume = 70,000 − 50,000 = 20,000 cases. Profit = 20,000 × 12,000 = 240 million VND (break-even volume covers all fixed costs; every case above it adds its full contribution to profit).

MAC-094.q: Operating profit equals margin-of-safety revenue multiplied by the CM ratio.
MAC-094.e: True. All contribution from revenue above break-even is profit.
MAC-094.x:
Basis: CVP analysis.
Analysis: True. Sales up to break-even generate contribution that just covers fixed costs; sales beyond it (the margin of safety) turn contribution into profit: profit = safety sales × CM ratio. E.g., MAC-014: (2,000 − 1,500) × 40% = 200 million.

MAC-095.q: Option A: fixed 200 million, variable 6,000 per unit. Option B (automation): fixed 320 million, variable 4,000 per unit. What is the indifference volume (units)?
MAC-095.x:
Basis: CVP analysis (indifference point between cost structures).
Working: 200 + 0.006x = 320 + 0.004x (million VND) → 0.002x = 120 → x = 60,000 units.
Check: A = 200 + 360 = 560; B = 320 + 240 = 560 million.

MAC-096.q: Option A: fixed cost 200 million, variable cost VND 6,000/unit. Option B (automation): fixed cost 320 million, variable cost 4,000/unit (indifference point 60,000). If expected volume is 80,000 units, the lower-cost option is:
MAC-096.e: Above the indifference volume, the high-fixed/low-variable structure wins, at the price of greater risk if volume falls.
o: Option B (high fixed, low variable cost)
MAC-096.x:
Basis: CVP analysis.
Analysis: At 80,000 units: A = 200 + 80,000 × 0.006 = 680 million; B = 320 + 80,000 × 0.004 = 640 million → B is 40 million cheaper. Above the 60,000 indifference point, high-fixed/low-variable structures win; but B has higher operating leverage and more risk if volume drops below 60,000.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

MAC-097.q: Consider these statements on CVP analysis:
MAC-097.e: Higher fixed costs raise break-even; CVP is reliable only within the relevant range.
o: Break-even is the activity level where total contribution equals total fixed costs.
The higher the margin of safety ratio, the lower the risk of loss if revenue falls.
Higher fixed costs lower the break-even point.
CVP is always accurate outside the relevant range.
MAC-097.x:
Basis: CVP analysis.
Analysis: True: break-even is where total contribution equals total fixed costs; a higher margin of safety means lower loss risk if sales fall. False: higher fixed costs raise break-even (MAC-088); CVP is reliable only within the relevant range – outside it fixed costs step up and prices and variable costs change.

MAC-098.q: Per unit: direct materials 20,000, direct labour 8,000, variable overhead 4,000 VND; fixed production overhead 600 million per period, output 50,000 units. What is unit cost under absorption costing (VND)?
MAC-098.x:
Basis: Cost accounting; VAS 02 (absorption costing).
Working: Fixed overhead per unit = 600,000,000 / 50,000 = 12,000. Absorption cost = 20,000 + 8,000 + 4,000 + 12,000 = 44,000 VND.
Note: VAS 02 allocates fixed overheads on normal capacity; if actual output is lower, unallocated fixed overheads go to COGS for the period.

MAC-099.q: Per unit: direct materials 20,000, direct labour 8,000, variable overhead 4,000 (VND); fixed production overhead 600 million per period, output 50,000 units. What is unit cost under variable costing (VND)?
MAC-099.e: 20,000 + 8,000 + 4,000 = 32,000 VND; fixed production overhead is expensed in the period.
MAC-099.x:
Basis: Cost accounting (variable costing).
Working: Variable product cost = 20,000 + 8,000 + 4,000 = 32,000 VND; the 600 million fixed overhead is a period expense.
Note: The 12,000-per-unit gap versus absorption cost (MAC-098) drives the profit difference between the methods when stock changes (MAC-020).

MAC-100.q: This period 50,000 units are produced and 55,000 sold; opening inventory of 5,000 units carries fixed overhead of VND 12,000 per unit (rate unchanged). By how much does variable-costing profit exceed absorption-costing profit (VND million)?
MAC-100.e: Inventory falls by 5,000 units → absorption costing releases 5,000 × 12,000 = 60 million of prior-period fixed overhead → absorption profit is 60 million lower.
MAC-100.x:
Basis: Cost accounting (profit reconciliation).
Working: Stock falls by 55,000 − 50,000 = 5,000 units → absorption costing releases 5,000 × 12,000 = 60 million of prior-period fixed overhead into COGS → variable-costing profit is 60 million VND higher.

MAC-101.q: When sales exceed production (inventory falls), variable-costing profit exceeds absorption-costing profit.
MAC-101.e: True. Absorption costing releases fixed overhead held in opening inventory.
MAC-101.x:
Basis: Cost accounting.
Analysis: True. When sales exceed production, stock falls: absorption costing releases fixed overhead held in opening stock into this period's COGS on top of current fixed overhead → absorption profit is below variable profit (MAC-100). The reverse holds when stock rises (MAC-020).

MAC-102.q: Weighted average method: 8,000 units completed; closing WIP 2,000 units, 50% complete for conversion. What are the equivalent units for conversion costs?
MAC-102.x:
Basis: Process costing (weighted average).
Working: Equivalent units (conversion) = completed 8,000 + WIP 2,000 × 50% = 8,000 + 1,000 = 9,000.
Note: If materials are added at the start, WIP counts 100% → 10,000 equivalent units for materials.

MAC-103.q: Total conversion costs (opening WIP + incurred) VND 180 million; equivalent units 9,000. What is conversion cost per equivalent unit (VND)?
MAC-103.x:
Basis: Process costing.
Working: Conversion cost per equivalent unit = 180,000,000 / 9,000 = 20,000 VND. Allocation: finished 8,000 × 20,000 = 160 million; WIP 1,000 × 20,000 = 20 million.

MAC-104.q: The difference of FIFO versus weighted average in process costing is:
MAC-104.e: FIFO separates prior- and current-period costs, showing current efficiency more clearly.
o: Equivalent units count only work done this period, excluding prior-period work on opening WIP
FIFO pools opening and current costs
FIFO is used only for job costing
MAC-104.x:
Basis: Process costing (FIFO versus weighted average).
Analysis: FIFO counts equivalent units only for work done this period: completing opening WIP + units started and finished + closing WIP; opening WIP cost is kept separate. Weighted average pools opening and current costs. FIFO shows current-period cost performance more clearly.
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

MAC-105.q: The setup activity rate is VND 300,000 per setup. Product X uses 120 setups a year. How much setup cost is allocated to X (VND million)?
MAC-105.x:
Basis: Activity-based costing (ABC).
Working: Set-up cost assigned to X = 120 set-ups × 300,000 = 36,000,000 VND = 36 million VND (rate from MAC-023).

MAC-106.q: Under ABC, product X is allocated VND 36 million of setup cost and 24 million of inspection cost; X output is 10,000 units. What overhead is allocated per unit of X (VND)?
MAC-106.x:
Basis: Activity-based costing (ABC).
Working: Overhead per unit of X = (36 + 24) million / 10,000 = 60,000,000 / 10,000 = 6,000 VND.

MAC-107.q: Compared with traditional volume-based allocation, ABC usually shifts overhead from high-volume simple products to low-volume complex products.
MAC-107.e: True. Traditional allocation often cross-subsidises, making niche products look more profitable than they are.
MAC-107.x:
Basis: Activity-based costing (Cooper & Kaplan).
Analysis: True. Volume-based allocation (labour or machine hours) assumes overheads scale with volume, whereas many activities (set-ups, batch inspections, order handling) are driven by batches and complexity. Low-volume, complex products consume many activities but get little allocation → cross-subsidy. ABC moves costs to their causes, exposing truly unprofitable products.

MAC-108.q: Joint costs VND 600 million. At split-off: X 30,000 litres at 15,000 per litre; Y 10,000 litres at 45,000 per litre. Using sales value at split-off, how much does X receive (VND million)?
MAC-108.e: X value = 450 million, Y = 450 million → each gets 50% = 300 million VND.
MAC-108.x:
Basis: Joint product costing (sales value at split-off).
Working: X's value = 30,000 × 15,000 = 450 million; Y = 10,000 × 45,000 = 450 million; total 900 → each gets 50% × 600 = 300 million VND.
Note: Versus the physical method (MAC-025: X gets 450 million), the value method matches costs to revenue-generating ability.

MAC-109.q: In process costing, normal loss is treated by:
MAC-109.e: Only abnormal loss is expensed in the period.
o: Including it in the cost of good output
Expensing it immediately as other expense
MAC-109.x:
Basis: Process costing; VAS 02.
Analysis: Normal loss (unavoidable under efficient conditions) is part of the cost of making good output → included in good units' cost.
Distractors: B applies to abnormal loss (MAC-110); C and D are wrong.

MAC-110.q: Abnormal loss is valued at the same unit cost as good output and charged to profit or loss in the period.
MAC-110.e: True. Abnormal loss must not inflate inventory cost; consistent with VAS 02.
MAC-110.x:
Basis: Process costing; VAS 02 (abnormal waste excluded from cost).
Analysis: True. Abnormal loss is valued like good units (same unit cost) then charged to profit or loss for the period – keeping inefficiency out of inventory cost. Consistent with VAS 02: abnormal waste is expensed in the period (ACC-026); it's also a signal to investigate.

MAC-111.q: Credit sales were VND 1,000 million in October and 1,200 million in November. 60% is collected in the month of sale, 40% the next month. What are November cash collections (VND million)?
MAC-111.x:
Basis: Cash budgeting (collections schedule).
Working: November receipts = 60% × November sales + 40% × October sales = 60% × 1,200 + 40% × 1,000 = 720 + 400 = 1,120 million VND.
Note: End-November receivables = 40% × 1,200 = 480 million (collected in December).

MAC-112.q: Required production 51,000 cases; standard 0.2 labour hours per case; rate VND 50,000 per hour. What is the direct labour budget (VND million)?
MAC-112.x:
Basis: Production budgeting (direct labour budget).
Working: Hours = 51,000 × 0.2 = 10,200. Cost = 10,200 × 50,000 = 510,000,000 VND = 510 million VND.

MAC-113.q: Static budget for 10,000 units: variable 10,000 per unit, fixed 100 million. Actual output 12,000 units with total cost 230 million. What is the flexible budget variance (VND million, adverse)?
MAC-113.e: Flexible budget = 12,000 × 10,000 + 100 million = 220 million; variance = 230 − 220 = 10 million (adverse).
MAC-113.x:
Basis: Variance analysis (flexible budget).
Working: Flexible budget at 12,000 units = 12,000 × 10,000 + 100 million = 220 million. Variance = actual 230 − 220 = 10 million VND, adverse – the part due to cost control.

MAC-114.q: Static budget for 10,000 units: variable cost VND 10,000/unit, fixed cost 100 million (total 200 million). Actual output is 12,000 units at a total cost of 230 million. Concluding a '30 million overspend' by comparing 230 with the static 200 is wrong because:
MAC-114.e: 20 million of the gap is due to higher volume; only 10 million reflects cost control.
o: The figures relate to different activity levels; compare with the flexible budget
The static budget is always wrong
MAC-114.x:
Basis: Variance analysis.
Analysis: The 200 million static budget is for 10,000 units; actual 230 million is for 12,000 – different activity levels, not comparable. Splitting the 30 million: 20 million from higher volume (a volume effect, reasonable), only 10 million from cost control (MAC-113). Compare with the flexible budget.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the reason.

MAC-115.q: Actual machine hours 2,000; actual variable overhead VND 21 million; standard rate 10,000 per hour. What is the variable overhead spending variance (VND, adverse)?
MAC-115.x:
Basis: Variable overhead variance analysis.
Working: Spending variance = actual cost − actual hours × standard rate = 21,000,000 − 2,000 × 10,000 = 21,000,000 − 20,000,000 = 1,000,000 VND, adverse.

MAC-116.q: Standard hours for actual output 2,100, actual hours 2,000, standard variable overhead rate VND 10,000 per hour. What is the variable overhead efficiency variance (VND, favourable)?
MAC-116.x:
Basis: Variable overhead variance analysis.
Working: Efficiency variance = standard rate × (standard − actual hours) = 10,000 × (2,100 − 2,000) = 1,000,000 VND, favourable.
Note: Total variable overhead variance = 1 million adverse (MAC-115) + 1 million favourable = 0.

MAC-117.q: Budgeted fixed production overhead VND 400 million, actual 420 million. What is the fixed overhead expenditure variance (VND million, adverse)?
MAC-117.x:
Basis: Fixed overhead variance analysis.
Working: Fixed overhead spending variance = actual 420 − budget 400 = 20 million VND, adverse.
Note: With MAC-065: over-absorption of 20 million = a favourable volume variance of 40 million (440 − 400) less the 20 million adverse spending variance.

MAC-118.q: Material price variance VND 10 million (adverse), usage variance 10 million (adverse). What is the total material cost variance (VND million, adverse)?
MAC-118.e: 10 + 10 = 20 million VND (adverse) (assuming quantity purchased equals quantity used).
MAC-118.x:
Basis: Direct material variance analysis.
Working: Total variance = price 10 million (adverse – MAC-032) + usage 10 million (adverse – MAC-033) = 20 million VND, adverse (assuming purchases equal usage).
Check: actual 10,000 × 21,000 = 210 million; standard 9,500 × 20,000 = 190 million; a 20 million gap.

MAC-119.q: An adverse labour efficiency variance may result from poor-quality materials or machine breakdowns, not necessarily from workers.
MAC-119.e: True. Find the root cause before assigning responsibility.
MAC-119.x:
Basis: Variance analysis.
Analysis: True. Poor labour efficiency may stem from bad materials causing stoppages, breakdowns, waiting for supplies or poor scheduling (MAC-038) – not necessarily workers. Find root causes before assigning blame; misattribution demotivates and leaves the problem unfixed (MAC-036).

MAC-120.q: Arrange the standard costing control process:
MAC-120.e: Outdated standards make variances meaningless; review them periodically.
o: Take corrective action or revise standards
MAC-120.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (standard costing).
Analysis: Order: set quantity and price standards → record actual costs → compute variances → investigate material ones (MAC-037) → take corrective action or revise standards. Outdated standards (changed technology or prices) make variances meaningless – review them periodically.

MAC-121.q: Select ALL drawbacks of incremental budgeting (last year's figures plus/minus %):
MAC-121.e: Justifying from scratch is a feature of zero-based budgeting (ZBB).
o: Encourages year-end 'use it or lose it' spending
Requires every expense to be justified from scratch
MAC-121.x:
Basis: Budgeting practice.
Analysis: Incremental budgeting's weaknesses: (A) perpetuates past waste as the cost base isn't re-examined; (B) invites budgetary slack (MAC-122); (C) encourages 'spend it or lose it' at year-end.
Distractors: (D) Justifying every spend from scratch is ZBB (MAC-030), not a flaw of incremental budgeting.

MAC-122.q: Budgetary slack occurs when managers deliberately understate revenue or overstate costs to make targets easier.
MAC-122.e: True. A common risk in participative budgeting when bonuses depend on beating the budget.
MAC-122.x:
Basis: Budgeting practice (behavioural aspects).
Analysis: True. Budgetary slack: managers deliberately understate revenue or overstate costs to beat targets and earn bonuses. It's a risk with participative budgets where bonuses depend on beating budget (MAC-123). Limit it with external benchmarks, historical data and rewards based on absolute results.

MAC-123.q: The main advantage of participative (bottom-up) budgeting is:
MAC-123.e: In exchange, slack risk is higher and it takes more time.
o: Greater commitment and motivation of implementers, using front-line information
MAC-123.x:
Basis: Budgeting practice.
Analysis: Participative (bottom-up) budgets raise commitment and motivation – people help set their targets – and use lower-level detailed knowledge, closer to reality.
Distractors: B is reversed – slack risk is higher (MAC-122); C – they take longer than imposed budgets; D – senior approval is still needed.

MAC-124.q: A workshop has 500 workers; actual productivity is 28 units/worker/day versus a standard of 30; 30-day month; contribution VND 3,000 per unit. What contribution is lost due to low productivity (VND million)?
MAC-124.x:
Basis: Productivity variance analysis.
Working: Lost output = (30 − 28) × 500 × 30 = 30,000 units. Lost contribution = 30,000 × 3,000 = 90,000,000 VND = 90 million VND (assuming all output could be sold).

MAC-125.q: Machine capacity 11,000 hours. A: contribution VND 12,000, 2 hours/unit, max demand 4,000 units. B: 15,000, 3 hours/unit, max demand 2,000 units. What is maximum total contribution (VND million)?
MAC-125.e: Prioritise A (6,000/hour) over B (5,000/hour). A: 4,000 units use 8,000 hours → 48 million; 3,000 hours left for B: 1,000 units → 15 million; total 63 million VND.
MAC-125.x:
Basis: Limiting-factor decisions (MAC-041).
Working: Contribution per machine hour: A = 12,000/2 = 6,000; B = 15,000/3 = 5,000 → prioritise A. A max 4,000 units × 2 hours = 8,000 hours → 4,000 × 12,000 = 48 million. Remaining 11,000 − 8,000 = 3,000 hours for B: 3,000 / 3 = 1,000 units → 15 million. Total = 63 million VND.
Reverse check (B first): B 2,000 × 3 = 6,000 hours → 30 million; A gets 5,000 hours → 2,500 units → 30 million; total 60 < 63.

MAC-126.q: Segment Z: contribution 50 million, avoidable direct fixed costs 30 million, allocated unavoidable common costs 40 million → reported loss 20 million. If Z is dropped, by how much does company profit FALL (VND million)?
MAC-126.e: Segment margin of 50 − 30 = 20 million is lost; the 40 million common cost remains → profit falls by 20 million.
MAC-126.x:
Basis: Drop or keep a segment (MAC-042).
Working: Segment margin = contribution 50 − avoidable fixed costs 30 = 20 million – lost if dropped. The 40 million common cost remains, shifting to other segments → company profit falls 20 million VND.
Note: The segment 'loses 20 million' on paper but contributes 20 million toward common costs – don't drop it unless capacity has a better use.

MAC-127.q: Running at full capacity. A special order of 2,000 units at VND 26,000, variable cost 18,000; accepting means giving up 1,000 regular units with contribution 12,000 each. What is the incremental profit from accepting (VND)?
MAC-127.e: Order contribution = 2,000 × 8,000 = 16 million; opportunity cost = 1,000 × 12,000 = 12 million; profit rises by 4,000,000 VND.
MAC-127.x:
Basis: Special orders at full capacity.
Working: Order contribution = 2,000 × (26,000 − 18,000) = 2,000 × 8,000 = 16 million. Opportunity cost = 1,000 displaced regular units × 12,000 = 12 million. Extra profit = 16 − 12 = 4,000,000 VND → acceptable (also weigh relationships with regular customers who lose supply).

MAC-128.q: When accepting a special order at full capacity, contribution lost from displaced sales is a relevant cost.
MAC-128.e: True. It is the opportunity cost of capacity.
MAC-128.x:
Basis: Special order decisions.
Analysis: True. At full capacity, a new order displaces existing sales → the lost contribution is the opportunity cost of capacity and a relevant cost (MAC-127). With idle capacity, opportunity cost is zero (MAC-040).

MAC-129.q: The selling division is at full capacity, sells externally at VND 30,000, variable cost 18,000 per unit. What is the minimum internal transfer price (VND per unit)?
MAC-129.e: Minimum = variable cost 18,000 + opportunity cost 12,000 = 30,000 VND (equal to market price).
MAC-129.x:
Basis: Transfer pricing (MAC-047).
Working: At full capacity → opportunity cost per unit = external contribution = 30,000 − 18,000 = 12,000. Minimum transfer price = variable cost 18,000 + opportunity cost 12,000 = 30,000 VND = market price.

MAC-130.q: A division earns 30 billion on 200 billion of capital (ROI 15%); minimum return 12%. New project: profit 3.9 billion on 30 billion. If accepted, how much does the division's RI change (VND billion)?
MAC-130.e: Project RI = 3.9 − 12% × 30 = 0.3 billion (increase), while ROI falls to 33.9/230 ≈ 14.74%.
MAC-130.x:
Basis: Investment centre evaluation (ROI, RI – MAC-046).
Working: Project RI = 3.9 − 12% × 30 = 3.9 − 3.6 = 0.3 billion → divisional RI rises 0.3 billion (from 6 to 6.3). Divisional ROI after the project = (30 + 3.9) / (200 + 30) = 33.9 / 230 ≈ 14.74% – lower even though the project adds value.

MAC-131.q: A division earns 30 billion on 200 billion of capital (ROI 15%); the company's minimum return is 12%. A new project earns 3.9 billion on 30 billion (ROI 13%, positive RI). If the manager is rewarded on ROI, they will most likely:
MAC-131.e: This is goal incongruence; use RI or EVA to fix it.
o: Reject the project even though it benefits the company (13% > 12%)
MAC-131.x:
Basis: Investment centre evaluation.
Analysis: An ROI-rewarded manager sees divisional ROI fall from 15% to 14.74% (MAC-130) → likely rejects the project, though its 13% return beats the 12% cost of capital and benefits the company – goal incongruence. RI or EVA fixes this.
Distractors: B, C and D don't reflect the incentive ROI creates.

MAC-132.q: In the short term, when market prices fall sharply, a business should continue producing if:
MAC-132.e: Unavoidable fixed costs continue if production stops; positive contribution reduces losses.
o: The price still covers variable cost and contributes to unavoidable fixed costs
MAC-132.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (temporary shutdown decisions).
Analysis: In the short run, unavoidable fixed costs continue even if production stops. If price exceeds variable cost, each unit still contributes to fixed costs → producing reduces losses versus stopping.
Distractors: B is too strict – producing below full cost can make sense short term; C and D aren't criteria.
Note: In the long run, price must cover all costs.

MAC-133.q: The relevant cost of material in stock with no other use is its disposal (scrap) value, not its historical purchase price.
MAC-133.e: True. The historical price is a sunk cost.
MAC-133.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (relevant cost of materials in stock).
Analysis: True. The historical purchase price is sunk. For stock with no other use, using it for an order forgoes its disposal value → the relevant cost is the scrap value (MAC-134). If the material is regularly used and must be replaced, the relevant cost is the replacement price.

MAC-134.q: An order needs 1,000 kg of material. Stock holds 600 kg (bought at VND 20,000/kg, no other use, scrap value 5,000/kg); the other 400 kg must be bought at 25,000/kg. What is the relevant material cost (VND)?
MAC-134.x:
Basis: Management accounting practice (relevant costs).
Working: 600 kg in stock with no other use → opportunity cost = scrap value 600 × 5,000 = 3 million (the 20,000 purchase price is sunk). 400 kg bought new × 25,000 = 10 million. Total relevant cost = 13,000,000 VND.

MAC-135.q: Select ALL qualitative factors in an outsourcing decision:
MAC-135.e: Book value is a sunk cost, not a decision factor.
o: Book value of the old machine
MAC-135.x:
Basis: Make-or-buy decisions (MAC-039).
Analysis: Qualitative factors: (A) quality control; (B) supplier delivery reliability; (C) protecting formulas and know-how; (D) effects on employees (layoffs, morale, Labour Code rules on redundancies).
Distractors: (E) The old machine's book value is sunk; only its disposal value (if sold) is relevant.

MAC-136.q: Match each pricing strategy with its feature:
MAC-136.e: Choice depends on competition, demand elasticity and product life cycle.
p: Low initial price to gain share quickly
High initial price for customers willing to pay more
Unit cost plus a profit markup
MAC-136.x:
Basis: Pricing practice.
Analysis: Penetration – low initial price to win share fast (price-sensitive markets, scale economies); skimming – high initial price for customers willing to pay, then lowered (new, differentiated products); cost-plus – unit cost plus a markup (MAC-071, MAC-137); target costing – market price sets allowable cost (MAC-050).

MAC-137.q: Unit variable cost VND 30,000, markup 60% on variable cost. What is the selling price (VND)?
MAC-137.x:
Basis: Pricing practice (markup on variable cost).
Working: Price = 30,000 × (1 + 60%) = 48,000 VND. Contribution = 18,000; CM ratio = 18,000/48,000 = 37.5%.
Note: A variable-cost markup must be high enough to cover fixed costs and target profit.

MAC-138.q: When demand is price-elastic (elasticity > 1), a price cut increases total revenue.
MAC-138.e: True. Volume rises proportionally more than price falls; but the effect on contribution must be checked.
MAC-138.x:
Basis: Managerial economics (price elasticity of demand).
Analysis: True. Elasticity > 1: the % rise in quantity exceeds the % price cut → total revenue rises. But higher revenue doesn't guarantee higher profit: consider contribution (unit margin falls), capacity and competitors' reactions.

MAC-139.q: 80% learning curve: the first unit takes 100 hours. What are total hours for the first 4 units?
MAC-139.e: Cumulative average: 1 unit = 100; 2 units = 80; 4 units = 64 hours/unit → total 4 × 64 = 256 hours.
MAC-139.x:
Basis: Learning curve model (Wright, 1936).
Working: Each doubling of cumulative output cuts average time per unit to 80%: 1 unit – 100 hours; 2 units – 80; 4 units – 64 hours each → total 4 × 64 = 256 hours.
Note: Units 3 and 4 together take only 256 − 160 = 96 hours (48 each).

MAC-140.q: The learning curve effect matters when pricing and budgeting early batches of new, labour-intensive products.
MAC-140.e: True. Ignoring it can lead to overpricing or biased budgets.
MAC-140.x:
Basis: Learning curve model.
Analysis: True. Early batches of new, labour-intensive products take far longer than once mastered (MAC-139). Pricing a whole contract on first-batch times overprices and loses bids; budgeting early batches on steady-state times understates cost and staffing. It matters less for highly automated processes.

MAC-141.q: Price VND 60,000 per unit, materials 24,000 per unit, 0.2 bottleneck hours per unit. What is throughput per bottleneck hour (VND)?
MAC-141.x:
Basis: Throughput accounting (TOC – MAC-051).
Working: Throughput per unit = 60,000 − 24,000 = 36,000 VND. Throughput per bottleneck hour = 36,000 / 0.2 = 180,000 VND per hour.

MAC-142.q: The first of TOC's five focusing steps is:
MAC-142.e: Sequence: identify – exploit – subordinate – elevate – repeat.
MAC-142.x:
Basis: Theory of Constraints (Goldratt).
Analysis: Step one is identifying the constraint (bottleneck) – the stage limiting system output; improving other stages adds nothing until it's addressed. Sequence: identify – exploit – subordinate – elevate – repeat (MAC-143).
Distractors: B is step 4; C builds WIP; D isn't a TOC step.

MAC-143.e: Invest in elevation only after fully exploiting existing capacity.
o: Subordinate other stages to the constraint's pace
MAC-143.x:
Basis: Theory of Constraints (five focusing steps).
Analysis: Order: (1) identify the constraint; (2) exploit it fully (never let the bottleneck idle; favour high throughput-per-hour products – MAC-141); (3) subordinate other stages to its pace; (4) elevate its capacity (invest) – only after exploiting it; (5) return to step 1 when the constraint moves, avoiding inertia.

MAC-144.q: Annual quality costs: prevention 50, appraisal 80, internal failure 120, external failure 150 (VND million). What share (%) of total quality cost is failure cost?
MAC-144.e: (120 + 150) / 400 = 67.5%: a high failure share suggests investing more in prevention.
MAC-144.x:
Basis: Cost of quality (MAC-049).
Working: Total = 50 + 80 + 120 + 150 = 400 million. Failure costs = 120 + 150 = 270 → 270 / 400 = 67.5%.
Note: Failures dominate while prevention is only 12.5% → invest more in prevention to cut failures, especially the 150 million external failures.

MAC-145.q: Consider these statements on the Balanced Scorecard (BSC) and KPIs:
MAC-145.e: The BSC balances financial and non-financial measures; too many KPIs dilute focus.
o: Financial measures are usually lagging indicators.
Training hours per employee is a leading indicator.
The BSC completely replaces financial measures.
The more KPIs, the more effective the BSC.
MAC-145.x:
Basis: Balanced Scorecard (Kaplan & Norton).
Analysis: True: financial measures are usually lagging – reflecting past results; training hours per employee is leading – driving future results. False: the BSC balances financial and non-financial measures rather than replacing financial ones; too many KPIs dilute focus (MAC-069).
